content_excerpt: Last week we shipped 7 launches across models, agent infrastructure, benchmarks, and science: two Gemini 4 models, our first Decision Model & API, self-hosted agent sandboxes, a new visual knowledge benchmark, and new robotics and genomics models. Gemini 4 Carbon , available as gemini-4-carbon , is our strongest reasoning model for repository-scale engineering, formal proofs, and cybersecurity defense. Gemini 4 Hydrogen , available as gemini-4-hydrogen , is our recommended upgrade from Gemini 3.8 Flash for everyday coding and fast agentic workflows. Hydrogen and Carbon share the same 1M unified context window, long decode architecture, and Interactions API schema. Pick the model that matches your reasoning depth, latency, and cost target: You can also pair Carbon and Hydrogen. Use Carbon to plan and orchestrate and Hydrogen to execute. The Gemini Decisions API , powered by Gemini Decision 1 , evaluates text, images, video, PDFs , or audio across up to 256K tokens against up to 1,000 isolated questions with 0 output tokens billed. Three question types return calibrated probabilities and a confidence score: noul for binary yes/no checks, choice across 2 to 255 discrete keys, and score for ordered rubrics. Pass media via base64, HTTPS URLs, or the Files API , and test rubrics in the Gemini Decisions Playground . Here's a runnable check over our sample WAV file: Gemini Managed Agents now supports self-hosted environments . We run model inference and the agent loop on Google infrastructure while bash commands and file edits execute inside your compute. Your worker connects over outbound HTTPS with a scoped key and zero inbound firewall ports. In production, you can deploy across Modal, E2B, Cloudflare, Daytona, Fly.io , Vercel, or Cloud Run using our self-hosted provider manifests . To test it end to end on your own machine, install our open-source gemini-api CLI from the CLI guide and run this single script. It creates a self-hosted environment via REST, spawns a local worker confined to ./sandbox , runs the managed agent locally, and cleans up the environment when finished. Local mode executes bash directly on your host unless you run inside a container or pass --disable-bash : We partnered with Artificial Analysis to release the Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark , evaluating 200 multi-step tasks across 10 verticals built around load-bearing visuals: CAD blueprints, RF schematics, GIS maps, gel plates, and charts. title: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
summary: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
summary: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

title: Agent-Native by Design: A Programming Language for Agentic Applications
summary: Building agentic applications requires combining large language model (LLM) operations, workflow structure and application state, and model-guided routing. With SDKs and agent frameworks, developers connect these components through supporting code that prepares model inputs, propagates state, and dispatches model-selected steps. Workflow changes can require coordinated updates to this code, increasing development and testing effort. Splitting execution logic between application code and framework internals also limits compiler visibility into control flow and state dependencies, hindering automatic optimization. We introduce Agent-Native Programming, which unifies these three components with shared execution semantics. We realize this approach in Jac, a Python-superset language, through "by llm()" for typed model operations and tool use, Object-Spatial Programming for workflow structure and state, and "visit ... by llm()" for model-guided routing. The routing construct derives the model's choices from executable workflow steps and schedules the selected steps. This explicit connection between model decisions and program execution gives the compiler and runtime a common basis for dependency analysis and automatic optimization. Across five benchmarks and five baselines, Jac achieves a 1.8-8.7x reduction in AI-integration code relative to the OpenAI SDK, with competitive observed task quality and lower coding-agent development effort. Two case studies demonstrate speculative execution and service partitioning through configuration alone, using program analysis and runtime checks to preserve workflow behavior under stated conditions.

title: vllm v0.34.0
summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

  • Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435).
  • TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418).

Serving and operations

  • Checkpoint/restore (CRIU + cuda-checkpoint) through /checkpoint/prepare, /checkpoint/status and /checkpoint/restore, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570).
  • Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down: dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370).
  • Best-effort NUMA binding on by default (#61258).
  • Opt-in cache-aware admission ordering (#54625).
  • Rust frontend: stateless Responses API (#63902) and n > 1 (#65625).

title: Why we rebuilt LangSmith around the agent
summary: We reorganized LangSmith around a single agent record. Build, run, improve, and govern every agent from one place, on any framework or runtime.
story_key: story|title:why we rebuilt langsmith around the agent
content_excerpt: Last week we announced our series C and introduced the new LangSmith Agent Platform : a single place to build, run, improve, and govern every agent. With this, agents are now the core object across LangSmith, connecting fragmented workflows for developers and enabling platform teams to manage agents across the business. In this post, we discuss why we reorganized the product, how the agent model works, what it unlocks, and where we're taking it next. 2026 brought a step change in agent adoption as new harnesses , models, and engineering approaches made it possible to build agents that can reliably perform complex, high value work . Companies now run many agents across the business: engineering uses coding agents, product is building customer-facing agents, and teams across the organization have various internal productivity agents. These agents are built with different frameworks, hosted on various runtimes, and use a variety of tools and models. Engineers work across disconnected surfaces. Tracing , monitoring , and deployments all live in different places. This requires frequent context switching, and in practice results in teams skipping difficult but important steps like building the evals. AI Platform teams have difficulty answering basic governance questions. Which agents exist, and who owns each of them? What do they cost, and how are they performing? When costs spike, there is often no obvious person to ask what happened. We wanted to make it simple for teams to manage the entire agent development lifecycle from one place, using any stack, with ownership and governance across all of it. LangSmith supports the entire agent development lifecycle: build, run, improve, and govern. Now, we've connected the entire process through a unique agent record. Each agent’s local, dev, staging, and production environments sit under the same agent ID, so comparing performance after making changes is simple. LangSmith is composable, so you can choose the parts you need. If you already run your agent on another platform, you can connect it to LangSmith to improve and govern it without changing any other workflows. title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control
summary: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
summary: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code , you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through. Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level. title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
summary: AlphaProof Code agents wrote three  million lines of proofs in Lean to verify Signal’s core encryption.
story_key: story|title:introducing alphaproof code a breakthrough in verifying complex software at dept
content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. title: aws-emulator
summary:
aws-emulator

Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so.

It's written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents - 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project. Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian wrote about how it came to be in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog.

It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms.

  • Fixed long options in lists and permission prompts being partly overwritten when they wrap, and first-run screens losing lines on narrow terminals
  • Fixed startup warnings about permission rules and the "N MCP servers need authentication" notice being recorded as seen when they were scrolled out of view
  • Fixed the welcome header showing control characters or splitting across lines when an agent's name or the working folder contains them or a line break
  • Fixed the red error shown when Claude tries a command only you can run: a dim line now says it runs only when you type it at the prompt
  • Fixed /stats showing an Active days total that was one day too high
  • Fixed /insights saying a report was ready when no session qualified for analysis, and writing two values into its HTML report without escaping them
  • Fixed /voice saying voice mode changed when managed settings, --settings, or the project's .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json kept it as it was; it now says what holds it
  • Fixed the IDE welcome dialog showing Cmd+Esc for Quick Launch on Windows and Linux
  • Fixed Slack app tips showing when your organization's policy denies cloud sessions
  • Fixed claude purge hanging silently when there is no terminal to read keys from, and its project picker and -i prompts ignoring the keyboard when stdin is piped
  • Fixed claude plugin eval --output-dir '' writing the report into the current folder; it now exits with an error
  • Fixed claude -p text output on a terminal passing control sequences other than text styling; pipes and files are unchanged
  • Fixed leftover .oauth_refresh.lock.owner.tmp.* files piling up in the config directory
  • Fixed /fast saying "Fast mode has been disabled by your organization" under the keyless Console sign-in, where Claude Code had not asked the server
  • Fixed /model saying that your organization restricts a model when Claude Code could not check that, for example with no network
  • Fixed "Sign in with your Console account" in /login replacing your existing login when you pressed Esc right after the browser step
  • Fixed the browser showing the sign-in success page in some cases where sign-in failed or was canceled
  • Fixed claude auth status and other short commands leaving a lock behind on a Console profile, which made the next session hang for about a minute
  • Fixed background sessions started on your claude.ai login using (and billing) an API key or token from the shell that started the background service
  • Fixed more cases of a session moving to another sign-in in the background; these moves are now refused, with a message saying what works
  • Fixed a second Enter in the exit dialog stopping background work after the move to the background was refused
  • Fixed token counting on Amazon Bedrock sending the conversation to Bedrock when the allowedProviders managed setting does not allow it
  • Fixed AWS credential_process helpers and Google Cloud default credentials failing when Claude Code is started without a HOME environment variable
  • Fixed a session sometimes going back to an earlier permission mode after a subagent's plan was approved
  • Fixed one invalid value in an Agent SDK applyFlagSettings() call silently discarding all settings from earlier calls; a call that would do this is now refused with an error
  • Fixed sessions showing as waiting for input when a finished pull request only needed your own review or merge
  • Fixed an unrecognized teammateMode settings value being ignored without a warning: claude -p, the startup warning and claude doctor now list it as a skipped entry (still not applied)
  • Fixed --worktree skipping a WorktreeCreate hook from a plugin in CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR on the first run in a new home directory
  • Fixed brief-mode sessions, such as Dispatch, sending a reply again after the turn had already replied
  • Fixed Claude saying a working Atlassian, Asana or Sentry connector had failed in cloud sessions when a plugin listed it at a different URL
  • Fixed Claude Desktop and SDK sessions listing a folder's own MCP servers (.mcp.json, local) as host-added or not at all, and not connecting WebSocket ones, after a folder move or pre-warmed start
  • Fixed /mcp still listing a plugin's MCP server after a plugin reload removed it while it was connecting
  • Fixed an MCP server staying "needs authentication", and its mcp_tool hooks being skipped, after a token refresh that was refused only for a moment
  • Fixed MCP elicitation requests being cancelled without asking in headless mode after a server's connection was replaced during a tool call
  • Fixed MCP tool calls from an SDK host answering "Not connected" after a tool call had reconnected the MCP server
  • Fixed an MCP task getting stuck after its question was closed with Esc or asked again: the footer now says it needs your input, and Enter in /tasks shows the question again
  • Fixed background MCP tasks that stopped updating after another call to the same server lost the connection, when a later call reconnects
  • Fixed a background MCP task's question opening over a message you were still typing; it now waits until you send or clear the draft, and the spinner and turn timer keep running
  • Fixed worktree.sparsePaths and sparse plugin and marketplace clones leaving out the repository's root files on older git versions, such as 2.34
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions with several repositories being unable to use a repository added mid-session
  • Fixed Claude asking for permission before reading your own artifact or its data
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules and hooks for the Artifact tool not applying in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts ignoring a worktree entered with EnterWorktree, writing ~ paths into the project, and leaving /mcp showing an MCP server as connected after its sign-in expired
  • Fixed words typed with a Yes at a permission dialog or plan approval not reaching Claude in Code Mode
  • Fixed Claude starting work by itself when you resumed a session that ended during a Code Mode script; it now waits for your next prompt
  • Fixed a missing OpenTelemetry user_prompt event for a message sent while tool calls run. The event has delivery.mode: "mid_turn" and the running turn's prompt.id
  • Fixed the OpenTelemetry user_prompt event leaving out earlier messages' text when queued messages merged into one turn in VS Code, or when one message had an image
  • Fixed a slash command's allowed-tools grants applying to background agents woken during or after its turn
  • Fixed /feedback and /bug to upload other sessions only when they were recorded by the signed-in account or organization
  • Fixed relative deny and ask permission rules (e.g. Read(./.env)) no longer covering the project after a cd; they now also apply in added directories
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules starting with mcp__plugin_*_ missing a plugin's MCP server or tool spelled in another letter case
  • Fixed deny rules not being applied to a permission approval that arrives after Claude Code restarts, in self-hosted runner and claude remote-control sessions
  • Fixed a case where a committed .claude/settings.local.json could be treated as the user's own when Claude Code was started in certain subfolders of a repository
  • Fixed some deny and ask rules not applying to certain Bash commands
  • Fixed a gap in Bash permission checks where some compound commands could run without asking; these now ask for permission
  • Fixed a case where a Bash allow rule could run a different program than the one it names
  • Fixed a connector tool's approval prompt in cloud sessions being answered automatically while plugins were still loading
  • Fixed some subagents changing an artifact that people outside your organization can see, or uploading files to it, without asking first when an allow rule is set or uploads were approved earlier
  • Fixed some artifact publishes skipping the confirmation for pages that people outside your organization can see when "don't ask again" had been chosen for Artifact
  • Fixed auto mode judging only the first change to an artifact that people outside your organization can see; its yes now covers that change alone
  • Fixed a managed strictPluginOnlyCustomization lock on agents and skills not taking effect in sessions that were already running
  • Fixed sandboxed commands being able to write to the native updater's download folder in some cases
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a worktree's settings and hooks
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a linked worktree's shared git folder
  • Fixed /teleport's stash choice in some unusual git states: it now stops and says what to do
  • Windows: Fixed a start-up stall that could last about a second when a PATH entry sits under a folder your account cannot open
  • Fixed /resume on Windows refusing or hiding sessions whose folder was recorded with a different drive-letter case or slashes
  • Fixed an in-session /resume on Windows dropping a project's saved trust when the session was recorded with a different drive-letter case
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when the working directory was below an allowRead folder inside a denyRead, such as under a symlinked home directory
  • Fixed Claude Desktop's third-party deployments staying on "Stopping" until a token renewal finished (once it includes this version)
  • Improved subagents cut off at the output token limit: they are now asked for the whole answer again, more briefly, instead of returning only its end
  • Improved startup with a keyless Console sign-in or other Anthropic profile login: a token that is still valid is read without waiting for the credentials lock
  • Improved the account email check: it now also refuses your email as a client's identity in scripts a command runs, file writes, web fetches and MCP calls
  • Improved the HTTPS authentication failed message for private plugin marketplaces: it now says git's terminal prompts and askpass programs are disabled, and it also appears with newer git versions
  • Improved the add-marketplace confirmations, plugin recommendation prompts and plugin install warning to say that plugins can run code on your computer, with access to your files and shell
  • Improved the claude --desktop sign-in error to name the API key, provider or setting that stops a Claude account sign-in from working
  • Improved the /voice "No audio detected" message on macOS and Windows: it now says where to pick your microphone
  • Improved MCP tasks: Claude is now told when a task is waiting for your answer, and can point you to /tasks
  • Improved claude remote-control: it now exits with status 4 when it stops by itself (single-session runs still exit 0) and 69 when it can't register, so a service manager can start it again
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session can't use its session's API key or token: they no longer suggest adding the key to settings
  • Improved the bundled dataviz skill's part-to-whole advice for static images and for parts with a natural order, such as age bands
  • Changed sandboxed Bash commands to follow the normal permission flow by default; set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true to keep running them without prompts
  • Changed managed settings that turn the sandbox on: to keep commands running without prompts, set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true in your highest-ranking managed source
  • Changed read-only git commands to ask first in a repository that isn't the project's or one you trusted; name it with --add-dir, not the additionalDirectories setting, to run them without prompts
  • Changed scheduled tasks and /loop to ask before running a skill that declares allowed-tools or hooks; add Skill(name) to permissions.allow to run it unattended
  • Changed "Always allow" in Desktop, IDE and SDK hosts: a rule alone is offered only when saving it would allow that command again, so a scheduled task that relied on one can now wait for you
  • Changed the sandbox to refuse sandboxed writes to .claude settings, skills, agents, commands and hooks in added directories, as it does in the launch folder
  • Changed worktree isolation: an isolated worktree session or agent is now refused git bisect run, git maintenance register|start and scalar's set-up commands, and is told what still works
  • Changed plugin MCP bundles (.mcpb, .dxt) to unpack under the plugins directory, not .mcpb-cache in the plugin's folder, so read-only plugin folders load; one fetched by URL downloads again once
  • Changed plugins of a remote marketplace that managed settings declare, enable and list in prependPlugins or appendPlugins to count as the organization's; pluginDigests is deprecated and ignored
  • Changed plugin loading to skip, and claude plugin validate to report, some unsafe paths and links in a plugin's folder
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders in --plugin-dir plugins no longer load from a session started above them; start Claude Code in the plugin folder instead
  • Changed EnterWorktree to refuse a WorktreeCreate hook path that goes through a symlink inside the project; have the hook print the real path
  • Changed tmux and iTerm2 teammates, and new sessions from the agents view opened with ←, to start in the session's folder instead of where the shell last ran cd
  • Changed prompt suggestions in the terminal to refresh less often after 8 turns in a row started by background or scheduled tasks, saving usage until you press a key or return to the terminal
  • Changed Esc on a background MCP task's question to "answer later": nothing is sent to the server, and the question stays in /tasks
  • Changed CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS to also set the context window of unrecognized model IDs that start with claude-, such as a gateway's claude-sonnet-latest
  • Changed /login to ask for permission to change your privacy settings
  • Changed /cost, $.session.usage(), --max-budget-usd and the cost and token metrics to count a mod's $.model.complete and $.model.classify calls
  • Changed the programs that Claude Code's sandbox starts for its own use, such as its network bridge, to run without Claude Code's sign-in tokens and API keys in their environment
  • Changed ripgrep, local git commands and the sandbox runtime's own helper programs to run without the mTLS client key's passphrase in their environment
  • Remote Control: Changed /resume and /teleport to disconnect first when the connected session has a share link, or when that can't be checked; run /remote-control to connect again
  • Changed Claude Code on the web, cloud scheduled tasks and Cowork cloud sessions to start despite sandbox.failIfUnavailable: the hosted container has no command sandbox
  • Changed requests for settings, permission rules, hooks or status over a cloud or self-hosted session's connection to return less or be refused; what applies in the session is unchanged
  • Changed claude -p with no cached account data to wait for that data before its first request, so a first run in a clean environment can start a few seconds later
  • Changed Claude's instructions to keep files you'll want out of its temporary scratchpad folder, which can be cleared
  • Changed marketplace ref to accept the full ID of any commit on a branch or tag; clients before this version can't clone such a pin, so a marketplace pinned this way stops loading there
  • Changed plugin marketplace and plugin downloads to use a CONNECT tunnel when ALL_PROXY is the only proxy set; a proxy that refuses CONNECT now fails them
  • Changed -p and SDK runs in a worktree or submodule mounted into a container to apply .claude/settings.local.json allow rules only once the folder is trusted
  • Changed self-hosted runners to refuse a session whose session folder or repository path is a symbolic link, other than a checkout hook's checkout
  • Removed "ask your admin to raise it" from spend limit and shared budget errors in cloud sessions and under Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Added prompt suggestions wherever the terminal shows them: Tab accepts the suggested next prompt; promptSuggestionEnabled: false in Claude Code's settings.json turns them off
  • [VSCode] Added a Console sign-in that creates no API key
  • [VSCode] Added a field to paste the redirect URL when signing in to an MCP server from the panel in SSH, WSL and container windows
  • [VSCode] Fixed the model picker's check mark staying on the old model after Claude Code restarted on another model or the model was switched over Remote Control
  • [VSCode] Fixed the effort selector offering levels above the effort cap set by your organization or the maxEffortLevel setting
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen offering sign-ins that the managed allowedProviders setting refuses
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for MCP tools not saying why Claude Code asks when a safety check raises the question
  • [VSCode] Fixed the message for organization settings that couldn't load saying to run a command again; it now says to try again, matching the tab's Retry link
  • [VSCode] Improved the note shown for an untrusted folder: it now says why the extension is off and how to turn it on
  • [VSCode] Improved the error shown when the system refuses to run Claude Code: it now says your IT team can allow a blocked program
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in card to say what to do when the browser shows a connection error for localhost
  • [VSCode] Changed the install link's marketplace confirmation button to "Trust marketplace and continue"
  • [Claude Code on the web] Fixed new cloud sessions cutting MCP tool descriptions loaded through tool search at 4,096 characters; the limit is now 16,384, as in other Claude Code sessions
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed artifact links pasted in Slack getting no card when the poster's Claude sign-in had expired in a workspace their organization doesn't manage; a plain card now appears

title: Kitesurf is now open source
summary: Kitesurf, our experimental browser engine for AI agents, is now open source. Inspect the code, run it locally, or deploy your own instance on Cloudflare Workers.
story_key: story|title:kitesurf is now open source
content_excerpt: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly: These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices. Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result. All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together. To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements , then clone the repository , install dependencies, and start the engine: The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787 . Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically. Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.
